"The hypocrisy is that on the one hand he's talking about the importance of preserving the Oval Office - which is legally meaningless because he can't do it - and on the other hand he is absolutely taking an axe to the law that allows us to preserve other historic sites."
Werkheiser notes Trump's efforts to renovate the Kennedy Center in Washington DC, to build a new triumphal arch in the city, and to paint the granite exterior of the historic executive office building. His firm has filed lawsuits to block two of the projects.
In October, the president suggested in an interview with Time magazine that the Oval Office would need to be torn down due to security concerns from the US Secret Service.
"I said, 'My ass, you can't build a new one. This is a special place,'" Trump said at the time.

title: U2 on Dolly Parton's final duet; and the 'grudge match' behind their new album
content:
U2 are at their best when they act on instinct.
Their biggest songs are fuelled by fiery indignation (Pride, Sunday Bloody Sunday) or sudden inspiration (One, Sometimes You Can't Make It On Your Own).
When they overthink, they misfire. An attempt to marry grunge and hip-hop on the 2006 single Get On Your Boots was, in the words of drummer Larry Mullen Jr, "a catastrophic choice".
So it was a good sign when, at the start of 2026, the band rushed out two EPs of new music, ripped from the headlines of a world in turmoil.
The first, Days of Ash, was urgent and angry – addressing the shooting of US citizen Renee Good by an Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) officer; and the death of Palestinian activist Odeh Hathaleenm, who was allegedly killed by an Israeli settler. Yinon Levy has been charged with reckless manslaughter and said he would fight for his innocence in court.
U2's follow-up, Easter Lily, was more reflective, asking whether faith and friendship are enough to sustain us in challenging times.
Together, they were the band's strongest material in years, combining the combustive power of their early, post-punk incarnation with the melodic sophistication they developed in the late 1980s.
"We put those EPs out without telling anyone," says Bono, the band's voluble frontman.
"Our management, our label, they all said, 'You can't do that, people won't notice'.
"And we said, 'We don't mind. It's okay not to have a big hype behind everything'.
"And it was really beautiful. The people who we wanted to notice, noticed."
For long-term U2 watchers, that's a big shift.
This is the group who described their 2000 album All That You Can't Leave Behind as the sound of four men "re-applying for the job of biggest band in the world"; and who forced 2014's Songs of Innocence into 500 million people's iTunes libraries - an epic act of overreach that Bono's been apologising for ever since .
There's no such hoopla around their new album, Carnaval de Luz, which is getting a pretty traditional roll-out for one of the world's biggest rock bands.
Sure, there's the requisite deluge of box sets and vinyl variants, a filmed concert for BBC Two , and a handful of interviews, including this one. But, more than ever, U2 want the music to speak for itself.
The album's a companion piece and a counterbalance to Days of Ash and Easter Lily. Inspired by ecstatic nights at music festivals, it rejects anxiety in favour of what Bono calls "defiant joy".
There's a stirring ballad titled If The World Is at War, We Better Not Be; while the chiming guitars of Superficiality lend an optimism to Bono's affirmation that, "the news can't break us".
"We didn't want to be dragged down by dark clouds or melancholy," explains bassist Adam Clayton.
"Our journey from the mid 1970s was about expanding freedom and opportunity for everyone: Make your own rules, pull down what wasn't useful. Now we seem to be in a period where that's under threat and under attack.
"We wanted to make the point that we didn't want our joy robbed."

title: Andrew received up to £2,000 per month from sub-letting, watchdog reports
content:
Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor was receiving up to £2,000 per month for sub-letting three cottages at his former home at Royal Lodge, when he didn't have to pay any rent himself, according to the public spending watchdog.
The Public Accounts Committee inquiry into the Crown Estate says the former Prince Andrew did not always rent out all the properties, so it cannot say how much the total might have been over more than 20 years of his time there.
The sub-letting income went to Mountbatten-Windsor, rather than his landlord the Crown Estate.
MPs on the committee have recommended that in future such leases should prohibit sub-letting, unless specifically agreed with the landlord.
Mountbatten-Windsor left his Royal Lodge home in Windsor in February, in the wake of revelations about his connections to the US sex offender Jeffrey Epstein.
He has consistently denied any wrongdoing in relation to Epstein and has been approached for comment.
The Public Accounts Committee has examined the leases on such royal properties as part of a wider inquiry into the management of the Crown Estate, which is an independent property company that pays its profits to the Treasury.
Mountbatten-Windsor had taken on a 75-year lease for Royal Lodge in 2003 and had paid about £7.5m towards its renovation and other charges, which meant that he did not have to pay rent.
But it emerged that as a tenant he had been intermittently sub-letting three cottages that were part of the property, which was thought to be for staff and at a below market rate, with Mountbatten-Windsor keeping the income.
The Crown Estate had told MPs that it did not have any oversight over how much Mountbatten-Windsor charged - and sub-letting was allowed as part of his lease.
But the MPs have recommended that in future the default position for such Crown Estate properties should be that such sub-letting should be banned, unless there was a specific exemption.
The Public Accounts Committee report also confirms what has happened since Mountbatten-Windsor's departure from Royal Lodge.
There was a payment of about £300,000 due to him for his early surrender of his lease, but because of "dilapidations" in the state of the building, there was a repair bill of £1.8m.
That meant the Crown Estate was owed £1.5m, which King Charles paid on his brother's behalf.
The watchdog's report also highlighted concerns about the level of rent being charged to non-working royals who had been given accommodation in three royal properties.
That was believed to be Mountbatten-Windsor's daughters, Princess Beatrice and Princess Eugenie, and Prince and Princess Michael of Kent.
A National Audit Office report had revealed earlier this year that Princess Beatrice and Princess Eugenie do not pay anything themselves for their accommodation in St James's Palace and Kensington Palace respectively.
The King pays their rent to the Royal Household from his own private income.
But the group of MPs were concerned about whether the level of rent on such properties for non-working royals was based on up-to-date valuations and recommended a more consistent approach to ensure value for money.

title: The engine parts that 'fight the laws of the universe'
content:
Every time you fly, an extraordinary feat of endurance occurs inside the aircraft's engines.
Hidden from view inside the sleek outer nacelle are hundreds of little turbine blades that can shrug off enormous mechanical stresses and temperatures exceeding 1,500C.
It is a true engineering marvel. And these hardy blades are not sculpted or cut from their material – they are grown.
During the 1960s, engineers worked out how to take a molten metal alloy, cast it into the shape of a turbine blade, and then cool it very carefully from one end to the other over a matter of hours. A single crystal or grain of metal alloy forms during this process of gradual, delicate solidification.
Like turning a cup of water into one big snowflake, of your own design, rather than a mini blizzard of many smaller snowflakes.
"It's about as complicated as manufacturing gets," says Ben Fifoot, manufacturing engineer at Rolls-Royce, which makes turbine blades in the UK. "It's a real motivator to get out of bed in the morning."
Only a handful of companies around the world can produce these single crystal turbine blades, and the process has been perfected end-to-end in just five countries, including the US and UK. Engine-makers continually vie for access to the technology.
Rolls-Royce, GE and France's Safran are among the few firms that have perfected the process.
In September, GE Aerospace announced it would acquire its turbine blade supplier for $11.75bn (£8.78bn). Neither company responded to BBC News' requests for comment but the move has been described as an effort to ensure supply of these critical components.
Separately, in March, Rolls-Royce said it would invest more than £19m in its Rotherham blade casting facility.
Turbine blade specialists continue to work on improving the capabilities of this little-known technology. All the while, China is desperate to prove that its engineers can produce turbine blades of the same quality as those in the West. Who will come out on top?
"Demand for [turbine blades] is huge. So few companies have managed to do it, which does give it this kind of magical aura," says Bill Sweetman, an aviation industry writer and consultant.
He suspects GE Aerospace's recent move is about securing reliability and predictability in the notoriously volatile aircraft manufacturing supply chain.
But why is the single crystal casting process, which has been around for decades now, still so specialist?
To grow one of these blades, asserts Fifoot, is to "fight the laws of the universe".
This is because each molten blade would naturally cool into a solid object consisting of many small grains of metal alloy, all jumbled together. But you don't want a crumbly sugar cube, you want a perfect diamond.
Getting a single crystal to grow into the shape of the blade instead isn't just a matter of cooling the molten version down slowly, the process also uses a bizarre trick called a pigtail.
The pigtail is a small spiral at one end of the blade. Fifoot says that, at the beginning of the cooling process, this spiral "chokes" the flow of solidifying crystals so that just one takes over. A bit like a hairpin corner in an F1 race right before the finish line – one driver can take the lead here and go on to win.
"Sometimes we need to play around with the number of turns or the angles on [the pigtail] to try and get more favourable grain," adds Fifoot. Once the blade is formed, this crucial but sacrificial spiral is cut off.
Blades made by Rolls-Royce are used in aircraft engines including the Trent XWB-84, which powers the Airbus A350-900, and the Trent 1000 XE, for the Boeing 787.

title: Pope begins lengthy trip to Latin America weeks after lung cancer surgery
content:
Pope Leo XIV is beginning a lengthy trip to Latin America just three weeks after surgery for lung cancer - a tour that includes a much-anticipated "homecoming" to Peru where he was a priest for many years.
The Vatican says no extraordinary measures are being taken in relation to the Pope's health, describing him as a "71-year-old who has undergone an operation" not someone with a "permanent medical condition".
It was Leo himself who revealed last month that doctors had discovered a tumour during a routine scan. The growth was removed along with the lower lobe of his right lung and his medical team then confirmed the cancer had not spread.
At a briefing in Rome ahead of the trip, which takes in Uruguay and Argentina as well as Peru, a spokeswoman stressed that Pope Leo had "fantastic stamina" and was "extremely enthusiastic" about the schedule which he had "personally confirmed... with no changes".
"The Vatican's message with this trip is, 'that was a short episode and now we're back on track'," Professor Massimo Faggioli of Villanova University told the BBC, pointing out that the Pope has had a busy return to work since his surgery.
"We have seen him in these last few days making speeches, audiences and so on. He seems in great shape. That was important."
The 12-day tour would be demanding for anyone, though. It incorporates multiple long-haul and local flights and covers thousands of miles from the Amazon to the Andes.
The starting point will be Uruguay, where the number of Catholics has fallen away steeply in recent years and which is getting its first Papal visit in four decades.
Leo then heads for Argentina, homeland of Pope Francis, his predecessor.
"This visit is also a homage to Francis, who didn't make it to Argentina [as pope]," says Father Fernando Laguna, the rector of Santa Maria Addolorata, Argentina's national church in Rome.
"When this visit by Pope Leo was announced, it filled all of our hearts with joy," he told the BBC. "I always thought he would go, despite his illness. I don't think he ever thought of calling it off!"
The priest is installing a big screen inside the church in Rome to allow parishioners to follow all the key moments of the trip from afar. The building is already decked out with posters declaring Pope Leo is welcome in Argentina. "We're waiting for you!", one proclaims.
This leg of the Pope's journey - which includes meetings with heads of state as well as religious events - could be the most politically sensitive. President Javier Milei once called Pope Francis "evil on earth" and a "communist" for promoting a doctrine of social justice to help the poor. In turn, Argentina's bishops have criticised Milei's harsh austerity measures, making sweeping cuts to social spending.
But Milei has already welcomed Pope Leo, writing in a post on X that Argentina awaits "with immense joy". Millions are expected to turn out to greet him.
The highlight of the trip is undoubtedly saved for last, when Pope Leo reaches Peru - described by the Vatican as a return to his roots.
"He knows these streets," is how a spokeswoman put it.
Born in the US, the then Robert Prevost spent almost 20 years in Peru, on and off, and even has Peruvian citizenship. That time is seen as fundamental to shaping his papacy.
His schedule includes a return to the diocese of Chiclayo where he was ordained bishop in 2014 and remained until Francis moved him to the Vatican almost a decade later.
He will also travel to Cusco, former capital of the Inca Empire, to say Mass more than 3,000m above sea level before heading to Pucallpa in the Amazon.
In all three countries, the Vatican says the Pope will have meetings with survivors of clerical sexual abuse - an issue which clouded a 2018 visit to Chile and Peru by his predecessor.

title: Democratic socialist defeats incumbent Karen Bass in Los Angeles mayor's race
content:
Democratic socialist Nithya Raman has toppled incumbent Karen Bass in the race for mayor of Los Angeles.
Raman's win stunned political watchers in California after she entered the race as a long-shot candidate against Bass, a political heavyweight who previously served in Congress and had never lost a race for political office.
Raman has frequently been compared to New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani. Both are democratic socialists and ran on progressive platforms.
Her win solidifies that America's two biggest cities will now be led by democratic socialists, which include some of the most high-profile politicians in the US, such as Mamdani and Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez.
Los Angeles was always likely to have a Democratic mayor but the question in the city - the second most populous city in the US - was just how left voters would be willing to go.
Bass, also Democrat, announced that she had called and conceded to Raman in a post on social media on Thursday, writing "while this is not the outcome we hoped for, the people of Los Angeles have spoken."
"Moving this city forward is what Los Angeles needs from all of us," Bass wrote. "I love Los Angeles. I believe in Los Angeles. And I will continue to ensure the promise of a better life belongs to all of us."
Raman, a member of city council and Indian immigrant, ran on a platform of change and fixing the "broken status quo and the politicians who failed them over and over again".
She ran on cutting homelessness, increasing housing in the city, saving Hollywood jobs from continued cuts and protecting residents from immigration enforcement efforts. Raman also vowed to fix the city's many issues, including helping beautification efforts, fixing roads and even helping bring back nightlife in the city.
The major issue in the race, however, was the LA fires, which killed dozens of people and razed neighbourhoods across the area in 2025. Bass faced intense political fallout over her absence during the emergency and the city's response to the disaster.
The next mayor in LA will oversee hosting the Super Bowl in 2027 and the 2028 Summer Olympics.
Raman entered the race as a long-shot candidate but slowly shored up support, especially from younger voters, before besting reality star Spencer Pratt in the primary race earlier this year.
Raman's win over Bass has all the appearances of echoing voter sentiment across the US as part of sweeping Democratic wins, including in deep-Republican country that hadn't seen liberal leaders in decades.
Washington DC also elected democratic socialist Janeese Lewis George as its new mayor, furthering progressive leadership in another major US city.
US President Donald Trump was asked at the White House about the wins by politicians on the left flank of the Democratic Party and said, "If you go by history, it's going to be a disaster".
Such candidates have become a focal point of attacks by Republicans.
Bass had been a prominent member of Congress before becoming LA's first black female mayor. Her roots are closely tied to LA and its history, even working as a community organiser during the violent 1992 riots over police brutality in the beating of Rodney King, who was black.

title: Delhi's toxic winter air is back - is the Indian capital prepared for pollution?
content:
There are two cardboard boxes in Meenu Rana's living room in Delhi. One is filled with Diwali decorations and twinkling lights. The other holds air purifiers.
"The mornings have already started feeling stuffy. It will get worse in the coming days, so it's better to be prepared," says the 43-year-old teacher.
She is not alone. Every year, as winter and the festive season approach, residents of India's capital begin preparing for something far less celebratory: months of breathing polluted air.
Delhi and its satellite cities record some of the world's highest pollution levels through the year. But as winter sets in, the air often becomes unbearable.
Falling temperatures and slower winds trap pollutants close to the ground instead of allowing them to disperse. Smoke from crop residue burning in neighbouring states adds to emissions from vehicles and factories, as well as construction dust. Firecrackers used during festivals often worsen air quality.
The result is noxious air and a familiar question: why does pollution return year after year, and why hasn't more been done to tackle it?
This year, however, the Delhi government announced its Winter Action Plan months before the worst of the smog arrived. The plan is in place from 1 November to 28 February, covering the months when pollution usually spikes.
Experts have called this a step in the right direction, noting that in previous years measures were often rolled out only after the air quality got too bad to ignore. However, they say this by itself won't be enough, calling for more holistic, long-lasting measures.
Just days after the plan came into effect, the city is slipping back into a depressingly familiar pattern .
This week, a grey haze hangs over Delhi, along with a distinct smoky smell that residents unwillingly recognise. People complain of irritation in their eyes and difficulty breathing, and coughs and sneezes are heard everywhere.
For those who can afford them, air purifiers have become a household necessity. Outdoors, people wear masks or cover their faces with cloth, trying to protect themselves from the worst of the pollution.
Tackling pollution was among the promises made by the governing Bharatiya Janata Party during its election campaign last year. Its winter action plan is now a major test of that pledge.
The plan restricts the entry of older, more polluting vehicles registered outside Delhi and denies fuel to vehicles without a certificate which shows they meet emission standards. Demolitions and outdoor construction work that generate dust have been temporarily banned.
Private vehicle use is being discouraged - the government has asked offices to allow half of their employees to work from home, introduced staggered office timings for its staff and doubled parking charges. It says it will also strengthen pollution monitoring and enforcement and promote public transport and electric vehicles.
These measures are separate from the Graded Response Action Plan (Grap), which is overseen by the federal Commission for Air Quality Management.
Grap introduces restrictions in stages, with stricter measures kicking in as pollution levels rise. This week, its second stage is in force, restricting the use of diesel generators and burning of coal and firewood.
Expert say on paper, these actions collectively provide a roadmap for responding to rising pollution levels but their success ultimately depends on enforcement.
"There are a lot of positive changes as far as planning is concerned, but when it comes to execution, we probably still stand at the same level," says Parthaa Bosu, strategic adviser at the Environmental Defense Fund, a non-profit group focused on delivering climate solutions.
Others argue that the problem goes much deeper.
"If we want to reduce pollution, we need to set targets for every sector - including power generation, industry and transport - not just vehicle entry, construction and stubble burning," says Manoj Kumar, an analyst at the Centre for Research on Energy and Clean Air.

title: Dolly Parton's scheme to send free books to children brought back
content:
A scheme set up by late country singer Dolly Parton, which posts a free book to children every month until their fifth birthday, has relaunched in parts of Wales.
Parton, who died aged 80 in August , was inspired by her father who couldn't read or write.
She set up the Imagination Library in 1995 and it's been rolled out in countries across the world.
But the charity has previously struggled in Wales, and there are calls for the programme to be "properly funded" for children across the country.
The Welsh government said it was "committed" to offering library spaces in primary schools and it funded a variety of schemes "to encourage reading for pleasure".
There are three school communities in Swansea that will be part of the new programme - Clwyd, Brynmill and Llanrhidian primary schools - as well as Pencoed Primary School in Bridgend and a community in Risca near Newport.
The scheme is aimed at trying to help parents and their children to access books, especially during a cost-of-living crisis.
Becky, 38, from Swansea said her nine-month-old baby, Phoebe, will benefit from the programme.
"We love it, we think it's amazing. I've got another little girl as well, Faith, and since she was a baby, we've read to her, and she is thriving now," she said.
"She loves reading to us instead. We buy her books constantly, so having a new one every month, she'll be waiting for it in the post."
Mum-of-three, Diana Cune, 34, said she encouraged all her children to read.
"I always tell my girls that knowledge is power, and books are the key to unlock that," she said.
"We're extremely lucky and I think this is a marvellous project for our community. The kids are very fortunate to have this project rolled out here."
With funding from National Lottery Wales, the scheme was launched at Clwyd Primary School on Wednesday.
There were performances by school pupils, as well as a Welsh language rendition of Dolly Parton's hit, Jolene, by singer-songwriter Bronwen Lewis.
The bilingual song, featuring Dolly Parton herself , along with her niece Jada Star, was released last month.
It followed the revelation that Parton has Welsh links in Machynlleth, Powys.
"It feels like a series of events have led to this," said Bronwen Lewis.
"From me singing in Welsh with Dolly Parton, her understanding her Welsh ancestry before she passed, and now a relaunch. It's unbelievable."
Across the UK, Dolly Parton's Imagination Library has gifted nearly eight million free books to children since launching in 2007.

title: Canada's federal budget includes billions for sovereignty and tackling homelessness
content:
Prime Minister Mark Carney has taken advantage of an oil revenue windfall to include tens of billions of dollars in new spending in his second federal budget, which focuses on building national sovereignty and addressing the high cost of living.
"That's what this budget does: it's the next big step in our action plan to make this country more independent, more sovereign," Carney said on Thursday.
"It focuses on growth, on people and that sovereignty, so we can live our lives as we wish."
The budget - titled Masters of Our Destiny - lays the groundwork for a Canada that is less reliant on the US for trade. It also aims to tackle the stubborn affordability crisis by promising billions to end homelessness and build new housing.
The C$142bn in new spending over the next five years is thanks to better than expected revenues from oil prices bolstered by the Iran War.
Canada's deficit is over C$50bn ($36bn; £27bn), with no path to balance.
Despite new spending, the budget shows that Carney has kept his previous fiscal goals intact.
The country still expects its GDP to grow modestly in the next year, outpacing all G7 countries except the US. Its unemployment rate, while unsteady month-to-month, is overall lower than last year.
But as people continue to feel squeezed by inflation and unaffordable housing, pressure has been building on Carney to translate his major investments into relief for the average Canadian.
And some sectors of the economy are feeling deep pain due to US President Donald Trump's tariffs on key Canadian industries, leading to thousands of job losses and uncertainty that has slowed business investment.
Here is a breakdown of some of the key takeaways for the 2026 federal budget.
One of the largest line items in Carney's second budget is an C$11.2bn commitment over the next four years to combat homelessness.
This includes funding for supportive housing, mental health and addictions treatment.
Statistics Canada reported last year that one in eight Canadian households have experienced a form of homelessness in their lifetime.
The government will also boost a grocery benefit that is available to low-and-modest income Canadians, which is estimated to provide C$2,570 for a family of four within one year.
Canada's opposition Conservatives have been pressing the Liberal government on  cost of living, and have routinely accused the prime minister of spending too much time on foreign trade missions and not enough addressing kitchen table issues.
There are signs that Canadians are struggling to make ends meet. Average hourly wages have not kept up with inflation, according to Statistics Canada. Food bank usage has hit record highs.
The average price of a home in Canada has dropped around 22% in recent years, mostly due to a clamp down on immigration. But houses are still too expensive for many in Canada's major cities - namely Toronto and Vancouver.
And like the rest of the world, the rising price of fuel has made everything - from gas to groceries - more expensive.
After hitting record population growth in 2023, which was fuelled largely by immigration, Canada has scaled back its newcomer targets significantly.

title: Will Atiku Abubakar be on Nigeria's presidential ballot after court ruling?
content:
Nigeria's Federal High Court has sacked the leadership of the opposition African Democratic Congress (ADC) party - and also ruled that the nomination of its presidential candidate, former Vice-President Atiku Abubakar, is invalid.
A statement from the ADC said the ruling was another desperate attempt to cripple the opposition.
Presidential elections are scheduled to take place on 16 January when President Bola Tinubu's main challengers are again expected to be Abubakar and former Anambra State Governor Peter Obi.
Several high-profile politicians joined the ADC in 2025 - disillusioned by the factional infighting in the once powerful Peoples Democratic Party (PDP).
Amongst them were Abubakar - who had served as vice-president between 1999 and 2007 when the PDP was in power - and former Senate president David Mark.
As accommodations were made for the line-up of political heavy-weights, Mark took over as its interim chairman.
But Nafiu Bala Gombe, a former ADC national deputy chairman, argued before the court that this was not lawful as Mark and others had not been elected at a national convention.
Instead, he said, he himself should have taken over the party's leadership following the resignation of the ADC's former chairman in 2025.
Interestingly, this is not first time the Federal High Court in the capital, Abuja, has ruled on the leadership of the party.
In July, judge Musa Liman said Mark had been chosen in accordance with the country's laws and the party's constitution - in a case brought by another former ADC member.
Abubakar said the latest case raised serious legal concerns: "Why, after that judgment, was another case filed to reopen the same dispute?"
In a statement, the ADC added that Thursday's judgement by Justice Peter Lifu was aimed at stifling the opposition momentum and "was a calculated attempt to weaken the ADC and frustrate" Abubakar's candidacy.
The ADC says it will challenge the ruling at the Court of Appeal.
In a statement on X, Abubakar, 79, said it showed the "panic was real" by those who felt threatened by his candidacy .
He said the timing of the judgment was telling as it came "barely a day after a mammoth crowd turned out in Sokoto [northern Nigeria] to welcome him" at the launch of his campaign.
"The people of Sokoto came out in their thousands because they are hungry for change and believe in our promise to make life affordable again. What we witnessed in Sokoto is only the beginning."
Political parties in Nigeria have increasingly been taking internal issues to court.
But as it stands, the electoral commission has issued its final list of candidates - and Abubakar is on the ticket for the ADC with former Rivers State Governor Rotimi Amaechi as his running mate.
The ADC is effectively the most powerful opposition to President Tinubu. Many influential politicians opposed to the ruling All Progressives Congress (APC) have already defected to the party.
The legal saga could complicate things - it may cause uncertainty for hundreds of ADC candidates as well as raise questions over who has the authority to represent them.

title: Who could be behind hoax bomb threats to European air travel?
content:
The warnings came in thick and fast, targeting one airline or airport after another.
In nearly all cases - London's Heathrow airport being a notable exception - they were taken to be credible enough to divert the aircraft in question, or even in Italy's case, to scramble fighter jets to escort it.
They all turned out to be false, which does not, of course, mean that the next ones will not  be real.
It is hardly surprising that the simultaneous, co-ordinated nature of these airline hoaxes, coupled with other malicious actions across Europe, are causing some people to point the finger of suspicion at Russia.
Following a series of cyber-attacks and mysterious drone sightings over sensitive sites earlier this year, in the past few days we have seen the remote hacking of supermarket freezers, as well as a blood bank, a suspicious incident on Poland's border with Russia, and in August a drone attack Germany's Leipzig Halle airport which its interior minister publicly blamed on Moscow.
So is Russia behind this?
There are many who argue, based purely on circumstantial evidence, that this must surely be yet another example of "hybrid", "grey zone" or "sub-threshold" warfare - actions that damage a nation's infrastructure or society but which tend to be anonymous, deniable and which fall short of triggering Nato's Article 5 and thereby mobilising a response by the West.
Moscow is certainly furious with Nato for supporting Ukraine and, in doing so, frustrating the Kremlin's plans to swallow up that country and effectively terminate its independence.
Russian bloggers have also suggested that, if Ukraine's drones are currently making Russia's airports unsafe, and Western sanctions are blocking Russian airlines from European airspace, then why shouldn't Western nations feel the same pain?
But as of Thursday evening no hard evidence had emerged linking the airline hoaxes to Russia, Iran or any proxy groups controlled by them.
There is the email threat sent on Thursday morning to airport authorities in Rome, purporting to be from "Fighters of the Male State".
That name likely refers to the Russian group Muzhskoi Legion or "Male Legion", an ultra-right group with such extreme views it was banned by a Moscow court in 2021.
Yet, it retained tens of thousands of online followers on Telegram as it cheered on the full-scale Russian invasion of Ukraine in the following year.
But the email sent to Rome, even if genuine - and who is to say it is not another group hiding behind that name? - is unlikely to provide the leads that police and airport authorities need to pin down who is generating these hoaxes and why.
For national police forces, airport authorities and transport ministries trying to work out who is behind these hoaxes and how best to mitigate their effect when they happen again, the task is not to go with who they think might be the most likely culprits but instead to follow the cold, hard leads - if they can find them.

title: California governor commutes sentences for state's 548 death row inmates
content:
California Governor Gavin Newsom has commuted the death sentences of all 548 people on death row in the state, changing them instead to life in prison.
"We can now let these offenders die in obscurity while we forever remember and honour the victims," he said in a letter.
The decision to spare death row inmates is largely symbolic in a state that has not executed an inmate since 2006, though experts say it could save millions of dollars in court costs each year. Only 13 inmates have been executed since voters reinstated the death penalty in 1978.
The decision comes as Newsom, the Democratic leader of the most populous US state, has been discussed as a possible 2028 contender for president.
Newsom, who is term limited, is winding down his final months in office. Fellow Democrat Xavier Becerra is projected to take over after the midterm elections on Tuesday.
Newsom explained in his letter that he is exercising his constitutional clemency authority to commute the sentences to life without the possibility of parole.
"After nearly 30 years in public office, I have come to understand the limits of what government can justly accomplish," Newsom said. "I take this action because I firmly believe that state-sanctioned killing is incompatible with California's values, undermines the foundations of our legal system and diminishes each of us".
California has historically had the largest population of death row inmates. Newsom had previously ordered a halt to the death penalty in the state in 2019.
Describing his decision as a difficult but "righteous action", Newsom said that although many Californians feel that those who commit brutal crimes deserve to die, he has concluded that "the state cannot morally kill them".
He said that by every measure, California's system for administering the death penalty "is a failure", and that it has not and cannot be fairly applied, resulting in the conviction of innocent people.
Life without the possibility of parole is the most severe punishment he can lawfully impose and that the state can ethically enforce, he said.
He acknowledged that his clemency action will anger and hurt some Californians and said that it will "always weigh heavily on me".
"As governor, I alone bear responsibility for this decision and its impact, just as I alone would bear responsibility for each execution," he wrote.
"For this reason, I am compelled to follow my conscience and, as authorised by our Constitution, take this action for the welfare of the State of California."
Because individual states have the power to prosecute crimes and order executions, much of the power lies with state governors.
Bernard E Harcourt, a law and civil liberties professor at Columbia University, told the BBC that it is not unprecedented for a potential presidential candidate to come out as an abolitionist in the run up to elections - despite the overall popularity of the death penalty in the US.
He noted that François Mitterrand did precisely that in his presidential campaign in France in 1981, taking "the higher ethical ground and was rewarded by the public for that".
"I detect a very similar ethical positioning in Governor Newsom's statements about the commutations. And here too, it may well be something that the voters respect," he said.
Newsom's decision comes after the high-profile botched execution of a woman in Tennessee in late September and while executions have been on the rise in the US. There are three executions scheduled for Thursday in Indiana, Florida and Alabama.
At least four of seven judges on the California Supreme Court will have to sign off on the commutations, CalMatters reported.
