title: Melania Trump calls for lasting Ukraine truce as she hosts Russian and Ukrainian officials
content:
US First Lady Melania Trump called for a "more enduring" ceasefire in Ukraine as she welcomed Russian and Ukrainian delegations at the White House following last week's truce in the southern region of Kherson.
Hundreds of residents of the Russian-occupied Ukrainian town of Oleshky facing starvation and constant bombardment were able to evacuate during a six-day ceasefire, which both Moscow and Kyiv credited Trump with brokering.
"The lives of innocent people must transcend the division of war. I hope Oleshky inspires greater peace," she said.
The unusual White House event saw senior Ukrainian and Russian officials meet away from the setting of official US-brokered peace talks they have been holding without success since last year.
The delegations were made up of Ukraine's human rights ombudsman Dmytro Lubinets and his Russian counterpart Yana Lantratova, as well as Ukrainian MP Davyd Arakhamia and Kremlin envoy Kirill Dmitriev.
Melania Trump was credited by all for playing a key though unspecified role in the ceasefire, and all parties conveyed to her the gratitude of the Russian and Ukrainian presidents.
The US first lady said she had "reviewed demining plans, aerial images, assessed roadways, and discussed evacuation routes, hospital access, vehicles, and medical resources" during the truce.
"Last week in Oleshky and neighbouring areas of Kherson, people experienced the simple joys of life for the first time since 2022," Trump said. "They walked down familiar streets without fear of explosions."
She thanked both Volodymyr Zelensky and Vladimir Putin, making no reference to the origins of the war, which began when the Russian president launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022, and which has caused thousands of civilian casualties and the displacement of millions.
Dmitriev, a businessman and Kremlin special envoy who has previously represented Moscow during peace talks with Ukraine, thanked Trump for "saving and touching so many lives".
"Let us continue making a humanitarian contribution together; this is within our power," Dmitriev said, before gifting Melania Trump a framed drawing by an 11-year-old Oleshky evacuee.
He also praised Trump for her work on reuniting children separated from their families by the war. These include children allegedly abducted by Russia.
Arakhamia, a Ukrainian MP who heads Zelensky's party in parliament who has also been part of the Ukrainian negotiating team, said the Oleshky ceasefire had constituted the "biggest de-escalation since 2022".
"We are creating a momentum where both sides are learning the… mechanics of how to actually keep the peace when the peace comes," he added.
He acknowledged that the "political track" of negotiations to end the conflict was "complex" but said Ukrainians were asking Melania Trump "to keep going and find new missions and de-escalate more."
At the end of the event, Trump  handed Dmitriev and Arakhamia two letters to be hand-delivered to their respective presidents.
The White House later said Melania Trump had invited her guests to view two historic artifacts which she had "personally selected as powerful symbols of peace".
One was an 18th Century medicine chest which was removed from the White House when the British set it on fire in 1812. "Once adversaries, the United States and Great Britain ultimately established a strong alliance," the White House said.
The second artifact was a cup gifted in 1899 to the French ambassador in recognition of his efforts to bring the Spanish-American war to an end.
Melania Trump has generally remained discreet on foreign policy matters, and neither Moscow nor Kyiv have elaborated on the nature or extent of her involvement in coordinating the delicate ceasefire - the most enduring and widespread of the war so far.

title: Eight killed in series of shootings in western Turkey
content:
Eight people have been killed and one seriously injured in a series of shootings in western Turkey.
The attacks took place in the Afyonkarahisar province on Thursday, with victims found in several locations in three separate vehicles, according to local reports.
The suspect fled, triggering a manhunt, and authorities later said he had been arrested in Eskişehir province.
CCTV footage published in Turkish media showed a man in a black jacket, white trousers and glasses clutching a long weapon as he stood by a red minivan.
Turkey's state-run Anadolu Agency reported that three people were killed near Ayazini village and three others near Kiyir village. In Yukaritandir, two women were found injured and later died in hospital.
Two teachers were reportedly among the dead.
Local media said roads leading to the affected villages were closed by police, while officers launched a large-scale operation to find the suspect.
The newspaper Milliyet reported that a vehicle allegedly taken by the attacker had been later found stuck in mud - the suspect having abandoned it before fleeing on foot.
In a statement posted on social media, the Afyonkarahisar Governorate said "all relevant institutions of our state have been working in coordination since the very first moment and are meticulously carrying out the necessary work".

title: Boebert, billionaires' tax and other midterms races still to watch
content:
Democrats have been celebrating their sweeping midterm victories, including flipping control of both chambers of Congress - but several critical races were still too close to be called on Thursday.
Votes are still being counted in two surprisingly tight Senate races in historically red states, Alaska and Mississippi, which could decide the true scale of Democrats' majority.
Several US House races are also too close to call, including that of Lauren Boebert, a prominent ally of President Donald Trump, who is facing a tight re-election contest in Colorado against Democratic challenger Eileen Laubacher.
Here are the races Americans are watching closely.
What and who are on the ballot: The race for Mississippi's Senate seat remains dramatically close with Democrat Scott Colom leading Republican incumbent Cindy Hyde-Smith by a little over 1,100 votes. The state has until 10 November to count  provisional and late-arriving mail ballots.
On the campaign trail, Colom focused his message on plans to address economic concerns, while Hyde-Smith, the first woman to represent Mississippi in the US Congress, was endorsed by Trump and campaigned with him.
Why it matters: If Colom wins, he would be the first black US senator elected in Mississippi since 1875 - and the first Democrat since 1982. Mississippi is a state home to the largest percentage of African Americans in the US, a group that overwhelmingly votes Democratic and showed up in large numbers this election.
What and who are on the ballot: It's another extremely tight race being watched nationally with Democrat Mary Peltola leading Republican incumbent Dan Sullivan by just over 600 votes with more ballots to be counted.
Peltola, a former congresswoman and Native American, campaigned for "fish, family and freedom", while two-term Republican Senator  Sullivan focused on his efforts to get Americans tax cuts and "unleash Alaska's energy potential".
Why it matters: The race has been marred with controversy because of the appearance of another candidate named Dan Sullivan on the ballot.
Last week, The New York Times reported allegations that Peltola and Alaska Democrats sought to confuse voters by recruiting the independent Dan Sullivan in order to siphon votes from the Republican Senator Dan Sullivan. Peltola has denied any knowledge of such a scheme.
What and who are on the ballot: Trump ally Lauren Boebert is trailing Democrat Eileen Laubacher by a narrow margin in Colorado 's Fourth District with 7% of votes left to be counted. In Tennessee 's reliably Republican Fourth District, Representative Scott DesJarlais is trailing Democrat Victoria Broderick. In Arizona 's Second District, incumbent Republican Eli Crane is leading Democrat Jonathan Nez by fewer than 4,000 votes with still many to be counted.
Why it matters: A loss for Boebert, DesJarlais and other Republicans in House races in Nevada and Ohio would mean an even larger majority for Democrats in the chamber - and a bigger rejection of Trump and his Make America Great Again movement.
What and who are on the ballot: California Proposition 40 would require a one-time 5% tax on the net worth of the state's roughly 200 billionaires to raise tens of billions of dollars in revenue. As of Wednesday, a million more people had voted against the measure than in favour, though only 61% of votes have been counted.
Why it matters: The measure would mark the first-ever wealth tax on billionaires in the US, which proponents say would raise $100bn for health care and education. But the proposition divided Democrats, with Governor Gavin Newsom opposing it.
What and who are on the ballot: For Kansas's next governor, Democrat Cindy Holscher is leading Republican Ty Masterson by a few thousand votes.
Holscher campaigned over escalating prices, while Masterson touted his pro-business, pro-agriculture, and pro-oil and gas credentials.
Why it matters: For more than 50 years, Kansas has elected governors from the opposite party of their predecessors. If Masterson wins, that trend would continue. Holscher's victory would break it by putting another Democrat in office after two-term Governor Laura Kelly.

title: Bonnie Tyler's hometown pays tribute with new mural
content:
A mural of Bonnie Tyler has been unveiled in her hometown as a tribute to the global star "who never forgot her roots".
The Holding Out For a Hero singer, whose real name was Gaynor Hopkins, died in a hospital in Portugal in July , aged 75, after undergoing emergency intestinal surgery earlier this year.
Hundreds lined the streets of Skewen , in Neath Port Talbot, where she was born and raised, to pay their respects on the day of her funeral.
Artist Steve Jenkins, who painted the piece at Skewen Memorial Park, said it was "important" and the "pressure was on" to get the artwork right for the community.
The mural features a large picture of Tyler's face, as well as references to the local rugby club and Total Eclipse of the Heart - one of her best-known hits.
Speaking to BBC Wales, walkers passing the mural described the tribute as "fantastic".
Susan Petrosillo, 61, from Skewen, said she was "very, very proud".
"It's absolutely fantastic what they've done. It's such a lovely park as well," she said.
"She was such a big part of Skewen and still is."
On 17 August, a celebration of life service was held at Swansea Minster ahead of a private family funeral in the village.
Petrosillo added: "On the day of her funeral, the hearse came through Skewen and the amount of people who came out for that was amazing."
For those who grew up alongside her, like Michael Davies, the mural is a chance to remember someone they knew long before she became a global superstar.
"I was in school with her, so I did know her quite well," he said.
"She was a Skewen girl, so it's tremendous."
Bob Marney, 84, said the reference to the local rugby club - an emblem in the corner of the painting - was particularly significant.
"The rugby club is where she had her first audition," he said.
"I'm really impressed [by the mural].
"She's a legend. She was down to earth, never forgot her roots. She never forgot Skewen."
For artist Jenkins, capturing Tyler's likeness came with "huge responsibility".
"I knew that I had to get it really accurate because of the emotions tied with Bonnie," he said.

title: Russell Brand found guilty of rape and sexual assault
content:
Russell Brand has been convicted of rape and sexual assault, and is now expected to face a substantial prison sentence.
A jury found the entertainer guilty of one count of rape and three counts of sexual assault, following a four-week trial at Southwark Crown Court in London.
He was found not guilty of two other counts of rape, and one count of attempted indecent assault. The jury deliberated for eight-and-a-half hours.
The 51-year-old was refused bail and will spend the weekend in custody before he is due to return to the same court on Monday for sentencing.
It can now be reported that Brand is also facing further rape allegations made by two women and has already been questioned by officers in relation to the complaints. The Metropolitan Police said its investigation "remains ongoing".
During the trial, Brand faced allegations from six women spanning the decade between 1999 and 2009, when he rose to fame as one of Britain's most high-profile entertainers.
The women came to court to reveal how Brand used his immense fame to force them into sexual activity.
Brand, who told his wife Laura Brand "I love you" after entering the dock, displayed no emotion as the jury delivered its verdicts.
Afterwards he mouthed "I'm good, I'm good" to his defence counsel as he left the dock. His walk was steadily paced, and he continued to show little emotion.
The judge, Mr Justice Bennathan, told Brand to expect "a significant custodial term" after the verdicts were delivered.
The jury found Brand guilty of raping a fan after meeting her at a 2009 stand-up show at the Hammersmith Apollo.
Brand was found guilty of groping an MTV worker during a party at a Soho bar in 2004, but not guilty of going on to rape her in a toilet.
He was convicted of kissing and groping a Choice FM worker after encountering her in a corridor at the Capital Radio building in 2004 or 2005.
Brand was also convicted by the jury of sexually assaulting a Channel 4 worker in 2009 when she had been forced to give him a massage.
Brand was found not guilty by the jury of raping a woman he met at a cabaret show on the fringes of the 1999 Labour Party conference in Bournemouth.
He was also cleared of trying to drag an MTV worker in to a toilet to indecently assault her in 2001.
Brand had claimed to be the victim of a media conspiracy to paint him as a sexual predator and insisted in court that consent was "more important than sex itself".
But he faced the compelling evidence of six women who accused him of crimes over the course of a decade.
Brand was also confronted with his own words from his 2007 book in which he claimed sex was a "birthright" and friends who revealed his relentless pursuit of sleeping with 5,000 women.
Mr Justice Bennathan ruled that Brand must be remanded into custody until sentencing on Monday, when he is expected to receive a lengthy prison sentence.

title: Major tech stocks plunge as US midterms add to fears of AI slowdown
content:
Hundreds of billions of dollars in market value has been wiped from major tech firms in the US and Asia in a stock market rout after the US midterm elections sparked concerns of a slowdown in artificial intelligence development.
Shares in firms across the tech and AI sectors plummeted following Democratic wins after election campaigns run on slowing AI.
The tech-heavy Nasdaq composite index closed down by more than 5.5%, losing an estimated $2.5tn (£1.9tn) in market value, according to Dow Jones data, while other key US stock indexes also saw big losses in their worst days since 2025.
The sell-off comes on top of broader concerns about whether the huge amounts being spent on AI will pay off.
In Asia, tech-heavy indexes fell sharply on Friday morning as firms that make the computer chips and other equipment that power AI saw their shares slide.
The Nikkei 225 in Japan was 6% lower in early trading as shares in memory chip maker Kioxia lost over 12.6% and rival Tokyo Electron slipped by 9.5%.
South Korean chipmaker SK Hynix fell by more than 11.5%, while Samsung was down by nearly 10%.
The sell-off in Seoul sent the Kospi index plunging more than 8.5%, triggering a so-called circuit breaker, a mechanism that temporarily halts trading to curb panic selling.
Taiwan's Taiex dropped by more than 8.3%, with chipmaking giant TSMC falling by nearly 8.5%.
It marks a "continuation of worries" over the level of spending on AI infrastructure, said MarketWatch chips analyst Britney Nguyen.
Democrats in races across the US campaigned to slow the growth of data centres and AI, and there were dozens of measures on ballots around the country aimed at restricting the development of the hubs crucial for powering the technology.
They won both the US Senate and House of Representatives in Tuesday's midterms, taking control of Congress for the rest of President Donald Trump's presidency.
Texas' Democratic governor-elect Gina Hinojosa campaigned heavily against data centres, pledging a moratorium on new construction in the sector.
In a social media post, Trump blamed the slide on his political opponents.
"The Stock Market suffered one of the Worst Days in History based on the results of the Election," he said.
"Remember, it wasn't Republicans, it was Dumocrats. Do not fear, however, we will soon, one way or the other, be BIGGER AND STRONGER THAN EVER BEFORE. MAKE AMERICA GREAT AGAIN!"
Some Democrats have argued that AI has grown too big without any safeguards or oversight and have promised, with their new power in Congress, to change that.
"Americans don't want Big Tech oligarchs wrecking the environment, gutting jobs and threatening humanity's future. NATIONAL DATA CENTER MORATORIUM NOW," Democrat Senator Bernie Sanders said in a post on X on Thursday.
Shares in companies heavily exposed to AI data centres, including crucial chipmakers and semiconductor manufacturers, fell sharply on Thursday, highlighting investor concerns that had already been growing.
Nvidia shares slid more than 9%, knocking more than $400bn off the firm's market value.

title: Three ways the interest rate rise could affect you
content:
Interest rates have been raised for the first time in more than three years - and it could be good and bad news for you.
Here are three ways the increase to 4% from 3.75% could affect you.
Rate-setters at the Bank make changes to interest rates to fulfil their role of keeping price rises at a steady level.
Higher rates are meant to encourage people to spend less, reducing demand for goods and services and limiting price rises.
This impacts businesses in two ways - less money to spend among their customers may mean they sell less, but also the cost of borrowing to invest as a company goes up.
Many businesses, particularly small ones, have variable rate loans which are influenced by the Bank rate.
Firms say higher rates limit their ability to offer new jobs and wage rises.
Mitchell Barnes, founder and chief executive of Ryse 3D, which manufactures 3D parts for the defence and automotive sectors, said the "reality" of rising interest rates was to look at the cost of employees and people.
That could include greater use of robots rather than workers.
"It's going to cause issues with, I suppose, employment across all sectors for people," he said.
"You're going to see reduced employment, more automation, more robotics being put into facilities, just in order to increase efficiency and make that money go further."
The Bank rate - and where it is expected to go in future - has a significant impact on the interest rates customers are offered on savings products.
So, if you're saving up for something quite expensive, like a holiday, or very expensive, like a home, then a rate rise could be good news.
When interest rates were low throughout the 2010s, the returns for savers were poor, but borrowing costs were low too.
The answer then and now, according to experts, is to make sure you move your savings to benefit from the best possible rates.
Leaving your savings in an old account (a product not offered to new customers), rather than shopping around, can mean you are penalised for your loyalty.
"Savers have endured years of unrewarded loyalty, with those leaving [a £20,000 cash pot] in closed accounts losing out on an extra £139 over the past three years compared to on-sale easy access accounts," said Rachel Springall, from financial information service Moneyfacts.
She also said locking away your money for longer, with a fixed-term deal, is usually more lucrative.
The other flipside is that renting while you save could get more expensive, because a rising Bank rate may well increase costs for landlords.
The big losers from a rate rise are those who borrow money, and specifically those on variable rate mortgages.

title: Six dead and others injured in fire at New York City building
content:
Six people have died after a large fire broke out in a residential building in Brooklyn, New York City, officials say.
Several others were hurt in the blaze, which occurred early on Thursday morning, the New York City Fire Department (FDNY) said in a statement.
More than 230 fire and emergency medical personnel were sent to the scene near Sunset Park after the fire was first reported at around 01:40 local time (06:40 GMT).
Mayor Zohran Mamdani said he was "heartbroken" by the deaths, and has asked New Yorkers to "take a moment to pray for the full recovery of those who were injured".
The cause of the blaze is being investigated.
A crew specialising in hazardous materials was sent to the scene because of the presence of a lithium-ion battery, although it was not clear whether this was linked to the blaze.
The emergency responders reportedly discovered on their arrival that the building's first and second floors had been engulfed by flames.
Four individuals were pronounced dead at the scene, according to the FDNY.
A male and female were also taken to the hospital, where they were pronounced dead, the New York City Police Department (NYPD) said.
Six other civilians were injured, two of them critically, along with three firefighters, the FDNY said.

title: Hoax bomb threats target European airlines and airports for second time in a week
content:
At least 21 aircraft and several airports across Europe have been targeted by bomb threats in the second such incident this week, with the UK calling it a "malicious hoax".
Flights to Austria, Belgium, Bulgaria, the Czech Republic, France, Italy, Poland and Romania were affected. An Aer Lingus plane from Dublin to Rome was diverted to an air base in France and Italian fighter jets escorted Finnair's Helsinki-Rome flight.
EasyJet said its flights from Newcastle and Glasgow were met by police in Prague as a precaution. London Heathrow and Birmingham airports received threats that were assessed as not credible.
No explosives have been found during searches, and it is not clear if the incidents, some claimed by a little known group, are related.
The airport authorities in Italy's capital Rome said the hoax threat against two inbound flights received on Thursday had come by email.
The warnings were signed on behalf of a group or individual calling themselves "Fighters of the Male State", claiming to be targeting a "feminist regime" and wanting to "make our mark on history".
They threatened to "turn the skies red" with explosions.
These details were first reported by Italian media and then confirmed to the BBC by Aeroporti di Roma, which manages both of the city airports.
"Fighters of the Male State" likely refers to the Russian group "Muzhskoi Legion" ( "Male Legion") - an ultra-right group with such extreme views it was banned by a Moscow court in 2021. Yet it retained tens of thousands of online followers as it cheered on the full-scale Russian invasion of Ukraine in the following year.
But that email, even if genuine, is unlikely to provide the leads that police and airport authorities need to pin down who is generating these hoaxes and why.
UK Transport Secretary Heidi Alexander described Thursday's incidents as "malicious hoax threats."
She said the government was taking "these threats seriously", stressing that there were "established processes for dealing with hoax and malicious threats".
A UK government spokesperson later said the threats reported "in the early hours" of the day had been "resolved", without giving any further details.
Heathrow later said in a statement it had received a threat earlier in the day which was "deemed not credible", adding there was "no risk to passengers, colleagues or the aircraft".
"There are robust UK aviation security standards in place to assess and safely manage these types of situations," the statement said.
Meanwhile, a Birmingham Airport spokesperson told the BBC it had received a threat, after which "processes were immediately initiated in conjunction with emergency services and partners".
The following flights were targeted by threats on Thursday:
Emily Noble, who was aboard the diverted Aer Lingus plane from Dublin to Rome, said she was about an hour into her flight to attend a friend's wedding in the Italian capital when passengers were told about a "technical" problem.
Later, as the Aer Lingus plane began circling for an unplanned landing in France, the pilot said there was a "security" issue, the 26-year-old from Dublin told BBC Verify.
On board it was "an odd experience," Noble said. "It was worrying because we didn't know what was going on, but we were all trying to be as calm as we could."

title: French protests see numbers surge as unions join strikes over high cost of living
content:
More than 600,000 protesters have taken part in rallies and marches across France, according to France's interior ministry, with five unions joining a day of action demanding more money for wages and public services.
The left-wing CGT union put the number of people taking part in Thursday's mobilisation at 1.57 million and hailed the figure as "a level unmatched" since 2023, citing big protests in Paris, Marseille, Bordeaux and Lille.
As darkness fell in Paris, Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu said he would convene a "social conference" with unions and employers next Monday.
The wave of protests began in September over poor conditions and resources at lycées (high schools), before spreading to universities, workers and a revived "yellow-vest" movement against high prices.
The unions had vowed to take the co-ordinated move against the government "to the next level", and CGT chief Sophie Binet had said their message was that "the only thing that will bring this mobilisation to a halt is responding to our demands".
Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez had earlier deployed 70,000 police, vowing "an extremely firm response" to any potential outbreaks of violence.
Some unrest was reported in several cities.
A car was set alight near the Gallieni bridge over the Rhône river in Lyon, as hundreds of activists from the radical left-wing "black bloc" clashed with police.
Clashes were also reported in the north-western city of Rennes, where the local prefect said a "hostile group of masked individuals" had gathered in front of the main union march. Tear gas was used to clear a square in the south-western city of Bordeaux and a teenager was hurt in a stabbing involving a student at a high-school blockade in the Seine-Saint-Denis suburb of northern Paris.
But the trouble was not on the scale seen during the last big day of protests, on Saturday 17 October, when more than 2,000 stores were looted and historic buildings set on fire.
The provisional numbers reported on Thursday were higher than on 17 October, considered  the biggest day of rallies until now when the interior ministry said 550,000 people had turned out and the unions counted 800,000.
Earlier on Thursday the leader of the CFDT union, Marylise Léon, said she would be happy if the protests matched that earlier level.
A coalition of unions across the public and private sector had urged workers, pensioners and young people to join Thursday's day of strikes to intensify pressure on the government. In particular they are seeking a rise in the minimum wage, or Smic , which is currently €12.31 (£10) an hour.
Sophie Binet told reporters at the start of a march in central Paris that protesters had "just reached a new level in their mobilisation" and were demanding immediate answers.
An estimated 9.89% of civil servants were taking part in the strikes, according to government figures.
Disruption was reported in schools, hospitals and public transport, and the Eiffel Tower and some exhibition rooms at the Louvre museum in Paris had to close.
Workers were also asked to halt production at oil refineries and France was expected to import more electricity than it produced on Thursday because of disruption at nuclear plants.
The head of the CFDT complained that it was not just the minimum wage that needed to increase. "We are asking for a net increase of €100 a month," Marylise Léon explained.
The government has sought to appease public anger over rising prices, bringing down the cost of fuel by releasing 10 million barrels of diesel from strategic reserves. Ministers have also promised school students to reform the unpopular Parcoursup university admissions platform and eventually replace it by 2028.
The prime minister said early on Thursday evening that Monday's "social conference" with unions and employers would seek to "provide answers to questions surrounding purchasing power and wages".

title: Food, fuel and taxes – can the Democrats actually make life cheaper?
content:
Two business owners, half a country apart, want the same thing for different reasons.
In Texas, Kim Hanks, who owns Tillies, a hotel, restaurant and spa business near Austin, says rising grocery and fuel costs are forcing her to raise wages for her 300 staff.
"It's been such a moving target for us on affordability," she told the BBC World Service.
In Indiana, Danny Reynolds, who runs Stephenson's of Elkhart, a clothing and bridalwear store, simply wants Washington to get its act together.
"My hope is that we can just find some consistency, some working together," he said.
Democrats say they heard both messages.
"We ran on affordability, we won on affordability, and now it's our job to govern on affordability," said House Democratic leader Hakeem Jeffries on MS Now's Morning Joe.
But here comes the difficult part. Democrats will hold Congress. Donald Trump still has the power to block their plans.
The scale of the win was bigger than most forecasters expected, with at least seven Republican-held Senate seats changing hands.
Behind the result was a striking mood: just 21% of Americans are satisfied with the direction of the country, even though the economy looks healthy on paper.
Voters weren't looking at the statistics. They were looking at their grocery bills, electricity bills and the price at the petrol pump.
In rural Texas, rising costs were even hurting Republicans in their own backyard. Sid Miller, the outgoing Republican agriculture commissioner, told me ranchers are getting $300 to $500 less for each head of cattle, while also facing record fertiliser costs.
"They felt betrayed," he said.
This was more than a blue wave. It was a vote about the cost of living. So what can Democrats actually do about it?
Under the banner "Fighting for an Affordable America," Democrats say healthcare is their first priority.
They want to bring back the extra financial help that made health insurance cheaper under the Affordable Care Act and reverse the cuts to Medicaid signed by President Trump in 2025.
Next come tariffs and energy. Democrats want to scrap the president's import taxes, which they say add thousands of dollars a year to the cost of groceries, fertiliser and building materials.
They also want to end the war in Iran, which they link to petrol prices averaging $4.18 a gallon, marking an increase of nearly 40%.
Housing is next. Some Democrats want to build four million new homes over the next decade.
On tax, they want to make billionaires pay more and increase tax credits for families with children.

title: Vance walks Trump tightrope with scathing election critique blaming Iran war
content:
Vice-President JD Vance sent shockwaves through Washington on Wednesday by blaming his party's midterm defeat squarely on the Iran war, in what was widely interpreted as an effort to distance himself from President Donald Trump ahead of a potential 2028 White House run.
In a carefully calibrated, 600-word statement on X, the vice-president acknowledged that Trump's 2024 voters had deserted Republicans in the midterm election .
"The reason we lost is the war," he wrote. "The president himself said so last night."
In interviews late Tuesday night and Wednesday, Trump had defended the war but acknowledged that it played a factor in Democrats flipping control of the US House of Representatives and the Senate .
Vance's view on the war in Iran is an open secret in Washington.  While he has repeatedly backed the conflict since the US and Israel attacked Tehran in February, he has reportedly expressed opposition in private meetings with administration officials.
But those disagreements had been kept out of the public eye - until now.
Hours after Trump and the party were handed a bruising election defeat, Vance made clear that he felt the decision to go to war was a clear political mistake.
"If you'd like to argue it was worth it, that losing the Senate for the next 6 years was worth it, then do so. Argue it was a worthwhile cost to pay. Agree or disagree, that's at least honest," Vance said.
It was a striking statement, and one with no recent precedent: it's hard to recall a similar moment in recent US political history when a sitting vice-president has so sharply broken with the president on a signature foreign policy issue.
Then came an arguably even greater surprise: Trump - who typically demands steadfast loyalty from his senior advisers - agreed with Vance that the midterms were "largely" decided by the war. He added that he would "do it again" if given the same choices.
It was an early sign that Trump - who has prized loyalty from his advisers - may give Vance a wide berth should he choose to launch a presidential campaign.
"I know how he feels about it. I think it was -- I think it was fine," Trump told reporters when asked about Vance's post blaming the war. "I knew that when I went in, and we stopped them from having a nuclear weapon, and they will never have a nuclear weapon."
Vance's statement seemed like "a way of separating himself from Trump," said Daniel Byman, a foreign policy expert at the Center for Strategic and International Studies.
Drawing contrasts with Trump will be a delicate balancing act if Vance seeks the presidency, Byman added.
That balance was on display in Vance's post. The vice president didn't mention Trump by name and attributed much of his election results analysis to unnamed pollsters.
Vance "put his toe in the water to see what he's going to do," Ashley Davis, a Republican strategist, told the BBC.
Beyond the Iran war criticism, Vance also offered a political roadmap that could preview a possible presidential campaign. He distilled the party's strategy to win back voters into a neat four-point gameplan:  "1) End the war 2) Focus on cost of living/inflation 3) Put America First 4) Change our relationship to Israel."
The list encapsulated much of Vance's worldview since bursting onto the national political scene, and read like the core argument in a future stump speech.
The BBC has contacted Vance's office for comment.
Of course, the next presidential election is still two years away. Vance is expected to run but hasn't made an official decision, and aides insist that he's still mulling it over.

title: Meet the unexpected winners of this year’s midterms
content: While Democratic victories in marquee national contests took the spotlight this week, with the party securing at least 250 seats in the House and winning back the Senate, several candidates in down-ballot races across the country clinched what appear to be surprising wins. Here are some of those winners: Nineteen-year-old Sebastian Matta will likely be the next Superior Court clerk of Maricopa County, Arizona, as he is leading his Republican opponent Jeff Dial, a former state lawmaker, by more than 85,000 votes as of Thursday evening, according to the county’s unofficial results . Matta, an Arizona State University student, would oversee an office that maintains records for the court that handles criminal and civil cases in Arizona’s most populous county. “I saw that nobody on the Democratic side had submitted themselves to this office in nearly a decade,” Matta told The Arizona Republic. “And I figured, ‘You know, why not?’” He told the outlet he never expected to win, but said he was “very overwhelmed with happiness” when he realized he had been a substantial lead over Dial. He’s has vowed to make the court more accessible, particularly for those that speak languages other than English. Dial told the newspaper he had called Matta to concede. In Georgia, 22-year-old Benjamin Culberson defeated his Republican opponent in a race for a seat on the Gwinnett County Commission by more than 10 percentage points, according to the state’s unofficial results . According to CNN affiliate WSB-TV , the Georgia Gwinnett College student flipped the seat, and the commission will now be made up of all Democrats. 19-year-old Daniel Darris-O’Connor , a student at the University of Massachusetts Lowell, unseated longtime incumbent Republican Marc Lombardo to win a seat in the Massachusetts House of Representatives. He’ll be one of the youngest lawmakers in state history. He acknowledged his age in an interview with CNN-affiliate WCBV , insisting that his campaign was focused more on the issues than the fact that he was a young person running for office. He recalled how the Covid-19 pandemic, which began when he was in middle school, was an “eye opener that the world isn’t perfect and we need new leaders in our government that are actually going to fix things.” Eric Armstrong, who suspended his campaign in September for an Iowa state House seat currently held by Sen.-elect Josh Turek citing health issues, is expected to win the race anyway as he is ahead of Republican Keith Jones by around 10 percentage points, according to the state’s unofficial results Thursday evening. In a social media post on Thursday, Armstrong announced that he would take office at the beginning of next year. “The voters of District 20 sent a clear message about the direction they want for Iowa, and I will make sure that message is carried to the Capitol in January,” he wrote. “Thank you to every voter who placed their confidence in this campaign. I will continue to do my best and be open and upfront about what comes next,” he added. Texas couple Marcus and Sheree Henderson will be the only two Democrats leadership positions in Kaufman County, which is in the northeastern part of the Lone Star State, according to county election results . Marcus Henderson will serve as Justice of the Peace, while Shree Henderson will sit on the Kaufman County Commissioners Court, a panel that votes on tax rates and oversees the county’s budget. A local news outlet reports that they are the first Democrats to be elected to the county in this century. Unofficial results show that pharmaceutical representative Christopher Russo won his race for county commissioner in Morris County, a Republican stronghold in New Jersey, by over 20,000 votes, becoming the first Democrat elected to a countywide office there since 1973, according to the New Jersey Globe .

title: Judges appear open to Trump’s push to overturn hush money conviction
content: Two years into his second term, President Donald Trump is still trying to wipe his 2024 felony conviction from the books. A panel of New York appellate justices on Thursday heard Trump’s legal challenges to his conviction on falsifying business records to cover up hush money payments to influence the 2016 presidential election. The five justices – who were all appointed by Democratic governors – at times appeared open to Trump’s arguments that federal election law and presidential immunity could affect the conviction. His lawyers argued the conviction tied to the reimbursement of hush money payments to Stormy Daniels should be overturned based in part on the argument that federal election law preempts state law. Trump’s legal team also says the trial judge ran afoul of the Supreme Court’s 2024 decision on presidential immunity by allowing testimony of White House officials and Trump’s tweets – official conduct – to be used as evidence in a criminal case involving unofficial acts. Trump was convicted on 34 counts of falsifying business records with the intent to commit or conceal another crime. At trial , prosecutors with the Manhattan District Attorney’s Office said that crime was to promote or prevent an election through unlawful means, which could include violations of the Federal Election Campaign Act (FECA), falsifying bank records, or tax crimes. “For purposes of the underlying election law conspiracy, the point is that (Trump) and his co-conspirators were really indifferent to the legality of what they were doing. They wanted to hide what they were doing, and to make these hush money payments without anybody finding out,” Steven Wu, Chief of Appeals for the DA’s office, said Thursday. The FECA violations were the most obvious ground for conviction, prosecutors said at trial, but Trump’s attorney Robert Giuffra told the appellate panel it’s actually “the most obvious ground for reversal.” “And the law is quite clear,” he said. “The Department of Justice and the Federal Election Campaign Commission have exclusive jurisdiction to regulate and enforce contribution and expenditure violations.” A jury of 12 New Yorkers found Trump guilty on all counts, making him a felon. Trump was reelected president , and days before his inauguration the judge sentenced him to an unconditional release. The panel Thursday challenged the state’s attorney on how heavily the trial team relied on the FECA violations to prove the 34 counts of falsifying business records against Trump. “Only partially,” Wu said, adding that evidence of Trump’s FECA violations were facts for jurors to consider rather than elements of the charged crimes. “What preemption does is prevent the state from directly enforcing a federal statute. That’s not what the prosecution was doing here,” Wu said. Associate Justice Bahaati Pitt-Burke pressed Wu further, noting the case dealt with campaign contributions. “That’s clearly within FECA purview. What are you using to get around that?” Wu said, “FECA is limited to direct limitations on contributions and expenditures. That comes from the cases, that comes from the regulation. But this prosecution and the statutes under which defendant were convicted are not about expenditures or contributions at all.” “If you think about the focus of this prosecution – the fraud that was committed in the records of a New York enterprise. That is not what FECA regulates at all,” the judge added. Giuffra leaned heavily on the federal preemption argument, but still said the appellate interpretation of the SCOTUS 2024 immunity decision could be precedent-setting. “It could be some other president down the road,” Giuffra said. “It’s not just about President Trump – it’s about future presidents.” Conversations with White House staffers and Trump’s tweets were both about unofficial acts and so not covered by immunity, Wu argued adding that even if the judge erroneously allowed the evidence there was plenty more to convict Trump. They were a “drop in the bucket” in terms of evidence of Trump’s guilt, Wu argued, so any presumed error would be harmless in light of the overwhelming evidence of Trump’s guilt. “Can there be such a thing as harmless error with regard to presidential immunity?” Justice Shlomo Hagler challenged. The Supreme Court’s immunity ruling determined presidential tweets can be official actions because that’s how he communicates with the American people, Giuffra said. Justice Troy Webber read from the Supreme Court decision and asked Guiffra how Trump’s discussions with former White House communications director Hope Hicks to respond to media inquiries about the payment go toward enriching Americans’ lives. Giuifrra said the tweets relate to Trump’s fitness for office. Other presidents have had to similarly defend themselves against allegations in public statements while in office, Trump’s lawyer added. Longtime Trump adviser and senior personal counsel Boris Epshteyn attended the proceedings as well, demonstrating the importance of the case to the president.

title: Melania Trump touts her diplomatic role as Russia-Ukraine peace eludes her husband
content: First lady Melania Trump hosted representatives from the highest levels of Russia’s and Ukraine’s governments at the White House on Thursday to celebrate the conclusion of a localized ceasefire — a humanitarian breakthrough, albeit limited, that came as President Donald Trump’s efforts to end the Russia-Ukraine war have so far failed. The brief ceremony — just two days after her husband’s massive midterm defeat that Republicans are blaming on his Iran war — highlighted the first lady’s positioning as a diplomat. Melania Trump and her outside senior adviser Marc Beckman — whom she and the foreign representatives credited throughout Thursday’s event — negotiated the three-day ceasefire in Oleshky, a Russian-occupied city in southern Ukraine that has been on the front lines of the war. Hundreds of civilians were evacuated, and humanitarian aid was brought in. “I was involved in every stage of the planning. I reviewed demining plans, aerial images, assessed roadways, and discussed evacuation routes, hospital access, vehicles, and medical resources,” Melania Trump said. Speaking in the Cross Hall, the first lady expressed hope that the ceasefire would be a “spark” that could “build a powerful flame of peace” in the war, which has lasted more than four years. Her husband had promised to end the conflict on “day one” of his second term, but he and his top negotiators, son-in-law Jared Kushner and special envoy Steve Witkoff, haven’t secured a peace deal. US officials are expected to mediate “working-level negotiations” between Russia and Ukraine next week in Abu Dhabi. As his ambitions for peace in the region have floundered, the president has faced bipartisan criticism for cozying up to Russia, especially in recent weeks after he waived sanctions related to Russian fossil fuel sales and again criticized Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky. The Trump administration and the Kremlin are also discussing sanctions relief for Russia’s multibillion-dollar sovereign wealth fund, whose CEO attended Melania Trump’s event. Kirill Dmitriev, a top envoy to Russian President Vladimir Putin, praised her “crucial leadership role” in the limited ceasefire. Dmitriev was placed under international sanctions by several countries, including the United States under the Biden administration, following Russia’s 2022 invasion of Ukraine. But the Trump administration first temporarily lifted sanctions against him in April 2025 to allow the State Department to grant him a visa to come to the US for talks on strengthening relations between the two countries. Russian Commissioner for Human Rights Yana Lantratova — who’s under sanctions by the US, EU and others — was also in attendance on Thursday. Ukraine’s Prosecutor General’s Office and Ukraine’s Security Service, the SBU, accused her of orchestrating the forced deportation of two Ukrainian children — an 11-month-old girl and an almost 2-year-old boy — from occupied Ukraine into Russia. Melania Trump has championed her role in the reunification of children separated from their families during the war, saying in October that she and Putin have had an “open channel” of communication. Thursday’s event came just hours after dozens of people were killed when Russia dropped at least nine bombs on a school building in southeastern Ukraine where they had taken shelter, Zelensky said, describing it as “one of the deadliest attacks of this war.” Zelensky praised the limited ceasefire on Thursday. “We’ve just had a humanitarian operation in Oleshky, which we coordinated together with the first lady of the United States. And this operation proved something very simple — when Putin wants the fighting to stop, it stops. There was real silence. No attacks. For some days. And we saved hundreds of lives,” he said at the Ibero-American Summit in Spain. Ukrainians also praised the ceasefire at the White House event, with David Arakhamia, a lawmaker and negotiator, saying, “We are creating a momentum where both sides are learning these little mechanics — how to actually keep the peace when the peace comes.” And Dmytro Lubinets, Ukraine’s ombudsman, presented state awards to both Trump and Beckman, who is not a government official but whose outsized role in the limited ceasefire was touted by both sides. “Without Marc, I think nothing would be happening. It’s 24-hour work,” Arakhamia said. Beckman, an advertising executive turned “exclusive senior adviser” to Melania Trump, helped negotiate her $40 million Amazon documentary deal and has advised her communications throughout the second Trump term, frequently appearing on conservative news outlets on her behalf. The first lady has made rare public appearances this term, choosing instead to engage behind the scenes in more substantive policy work. And while she actively avoided the 2026 midterm campaign trail because she prefers not to be involved in politics — and the West Wing did not seek her presence, sources told CNN — she’s been quietly focused on issues with more bipartisan appeal than some of her husband’s top priorities. Besides negotiating the localized ceasefire, her work has included lobbying for legislation aimed at protecting Americans from deepfake and revenge porn and advocating for children aging out of foster care.

title: Democratic socialist Nithya Raman will defeat Karen Bass in LA mayor’s race, CNN projects
content: Democratic socialist Nithya Raman will defeat incumbent Karen Bass in the Los Angeles mayor’s race, CNN’s Decision Desk projects. Raman, a city councilmember, overtook Republican Spencer Pratt in June’s nonpartisan primary to set up what was arguably a tougher race for Bass, a Democratic former congresswoman. With Raman’s victory, the nation’s two largest cities — New York and Los Angeles — will be led by democratic socialists next year. Raman has vowed to cut street homelessness in half before Los Angeles hosts the 2028 Olympics. Her victory highlights the continued ascendance of the Democratic Party’s progressive insurgency. Since last year, democratic socialists have won the mayor’s offices in New York, Los Angeles, Washington, DC, and Seattle. In Los Angeles, Raman’s win ends the tenure of a 73-year-old fixture of the party’s establishment who made history in the State Assembly in 2008 when she became the first Black woman to become speaker of any state legislative body in US history. The ideological and factional battles that played out in the Los Angeles race will soon expand nationwide, as the 2028 Democratic presidential primary gets underway in the coming months and the party’s leaders and voters debate whether what worked in mayoral races in deep-blue cities can succeed nationally. The victory by Raman, 45, is a harsh blow to the Los Angeles political establishment, including most major unions, which had rallied behind Bass. The outcome reflects the lingering anger at how Bass managed the fallout from the 2025 wildfires , as well as voters seeking new approaches to entrenched issues like housing costs and homelessness. Those were the same issues that animated Pratt’s campaign during the primary , when he earned 25.5% of the vote — about 3.5 percentage points behind Raman for second place. The two outsiders combining for more than 54% of the vote, though, underscored the difficulty Bass would face in winning a second term. This story has been updated with additional information.

title: Some Democratic Senate candidates would have won even if nobody voted for them on Election Day
content: How dominant were Democrats in the 2026 election? So dominant that they could have won some marquee races even if literally none of their voters showed up on Election Day. That was true in Senate races in Georgia, North Carolina and Texas. And it could also be true of the Arizona governor’s race. In each one, more voters voted for the Democrat via early voting and absentee and/or mail voting than voted in total for the Republican — including all methods of voting. In each race, the Democrat appears to have won by 10 or more percentage points. In Georgia, returns from the secretary of state show Sen. Jon Ossoff getting about 1,772,000 votes from early and absentee voting, compared to about 1,712,000 total votes for his opponent, GOP Rep. Mike Collins. Ossoff’s current lead stands at 18 points. In Texas, data from the secretary of state shows Democratic Sen.-elect James Talarico got 4.4 million early votes, compared to 4.25 million total votes for GOP state Attorney General Ken Paxton. Talarico surprised many by winning his race by double digits — in a state where Democrats hadn’t won a statewide office since 1994. In North Carolina, data from the State Board of Elections shows Democratic former Gov. Roy Cooper receiving about 1,728,000 early in-person votes, compared to about 1,643,000 votes total for Republican Michael Whatley. Cooper didn’t even need absentee votes to beat Whatley. His early vote total trumped Whatley’s total from early, absentee and Election Day voting. President Donald Trump came to the state repeatedly to try to help Whatley, and Cooper is currently winning by 20 points. He is the first Democrat North Carolina has elected to the Senate since 2008. The stats reinforce just how crucial the early vote is to Democrats, in particular. Democratic voters remained significantly more likely to vote early than Republicans in these midterms. In Texas, Talarico is currently getting more than 80% of his vote total from early votes. And in North Carolina, Cooper is getting 73% of his votes outside of Election Day voting. The early vote dominance could also be the case in a governor’s race in another swing state: Arizona. There, the latest results show Democratic Gov. Katie Hobbs getting more than 1 million early votes, compared to 960,000 total votes for Republican Rep. Andy Biggs. Hobbs currently leads in her reelection race by 11 points. Those numbers could shift, though, as the state has counted an estimated 86% of its vote. The numbers are particularly striking given all of these races were once considered competitive. Three of them are in presidential swing states, while Texas has long been a red state. And, if nothing else, the stats reinforce just how much US elections are now conducted outside of Election Day — and how parties could have major races in difficult states like these locked up before the regular polls even open.

title: Democrats’ House majority is trending toward historic
content: The 2026 midterm elections have clearly been very good for Democrats across the board. But their House majority is trending toward historic numbers. CNN is projecting that Democrats have won more than 250 House seats , with a net gain of around 40 seats. And they could hit or even exceed 260 total seats by the time all is said and done. That would give them around an 85-seat majority and make it the biggest Democratic majority since the early 1990s — the tail end of decades of Democratic domination of the House. After flipping more seats on Thursday afternoon, Democrats have won or hold leads in 259 districts. If those margins hold, Republicans would end up with 174 (two Louisiana races are headed to runoffs). Democrats lead by around a point or less in six districts: South Carolina’s 1st, Colorado’s 4th, Florida’s 9th, Minnesota’s 1st, North Carolina’s 5th and Tennessee’s 4th. If Democrats get to 260 seats, it would be their biggest House majority since 1991-93 , when they had 267. They had 258 seats in the following Congress and 257 after former President Barack Obama’s big win in 2008 swept Democrats into power. By winning more than 250 seats, Democrats’ House majority is already bigger than any Republican House majority since the Great Depression. (The GOP’s high watermark since then was 247 seats after the 2014 election). If they won 260, it would mean Democrats have won 60% of the available House seats. That’s compared to winning between 54% and 56% of the Senate (depending upon how the last two races in Alaska and Mississippi shake out). It looks as though Democrats will have gained somewhere around 50 seats by the time all races are settled. If they win the 259 seats where they’re currently ahead, it would be a net gain of 44 seats. That would be the third-largest gain in the past half-century, behind 2010 (Republicans gained 63 seats) and 1994 (Republicans gained 54). It would also surpass Democrats’ biggest recent midterms: the 2018 election (41 seats) and the 2006 election (31 seats). But drilling into the details, the number of seats flipped might be even more significant than all of those. The GOP flipped so many seats in 2010 in large part because Democrats had such a big majority after the 2008 election. That meant Republicans had lots of low-hanging fruit in conservative-leaning territory to go after. Republicans were also chipping away at a nearly 260-seat Democratic majority in the 1994 election. By contrast, the 2026 election began with nearly an even split in the House: Republicans at 220 districts to Democrats’ 215 . Democrats were also contending with the fact that Republicans redrew several of their maps to give themselves more conservative-leaning territory ( it didn’t work ). The other big metric here is the popular vote. Currently, Democrats lead by about 12 percentage points — a margin which could grow in the coming days as more votes are reported, especially from western, Democratic-leaning states. There are some caveats with that. It’s skewed somewhat by the fact that California’s top-two primary system means that a handful of races are Republicans-versus-Republican and Democrat-versus-Democrat — rather than having all 435 districts include votes for both major parties. But it’s still overall a good measure. This will mark only the second time since 1982 that a party won the House popular vote by double digits — with the other one being the Obama election of 2008 (an 11-point Democratic margin), according to data from the Brookings Institution . And the last time either party won the House popular vote by at least 13 points was in the post-Watergate election of 1976.

title: Vance, DeSantis make quick moves after disastrous GOP midterms jumpstart 2028 race
content: Vice President JD Vance’s seemingly straightforward path to succeeding President Donald Trump suddenly looks much murkier. The Republican shellacking in Tuesday’s midterm elections has quickly triggered a public reckoning within the GOP over Trump’s place in the future of the party — one that threatens to complicate Vance’s efforts to consolidate party support behind a widely anticipated White House bid. Vance appeared to recognize the danger Wednesday morning, blaming the party’s sweeping losses on the war with Iran and distancing himself from Trump’s unpopular foreign policy decisions. In a lengthy post on X , Vance appeared to sketch out what the foundations for his own 2028 platform, centered on ending the war, tackling affordability, refocusing on domestic challenges and reconsidering America’s relationship with Israel. “To the people who are just pissed at the results, you should be,” he wrote. “Let’s take that anger and get back to the work of saving our country.” But there are already signs that there may be a widening lane for someone outside the administration to seize the nomination in 2028. Former House Speaker Newt Gingrich wrote Wednesday on X that “the scale of the Republican defeat is so great that it makes the race for the GOP presidential nomination wide open.” In the post, he ripped Vance for defending an ad from Ohio Republican gubernatorial candidate Vivek Ramaswamy that featured the estranged mother of his Democratic opponent, Amy Acton. The ad received bipartisan blowback and on Tuesday, Acton defeated Ramaswamy. “A good bit of the luster has come off the bloom,” Gingrich wrote. Bob Vander Plaats, an influential conservative leader in Iowa, where Republicans will have the first say in choosing their next nominee, predicted the losses would embolden presidential hopefuls from across the party to test the waters. By next year, he said, the field could rival the crowded 2016 Republican primary. “There are a lot of people now who will be making the case they can take this baton and move us forward,” Vander Plaats said. A longtime Republican operative in New Hampshire, who asked not to be named, said the prospect of Vance running as a third Trump term looks increasingly “problematic” after Tuesday. The operative also expected voters in the nation’s first primary will give other candidates a serious look. Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis, in particular, has wasted little time seizing the party’s historic defeats to revive interest in his own political future. DeSantis unsuccessfully challenged Trump for the GOP nomination in 2024 and, before Tuesday, had seen his stock diminish as his time in public office came to a close. But DeSantis in recent days has received renewed attention for his pointed critique of Trump’s second stint in Washington. In a lengthy interview with Stephen A. Smith released on the eve of the election, DeSantis accused the Trump administration of gaslighting voters, failing to tackle Washington corruption and botching its immigration rollout. He challenged Republicans to rethink their relationship with Big Tech and heed growing concerns about data centers and artificial intelligence — a notable shot at an industry that is close to Vance. On Wednesday, DeSantis called the midterms an “extinction-level event for Republicans,” while touting that Florida “was able to hold the line.” Republican nominees for governor and Senate narrowly survived, but DeSantis’ efforts to net his party more congressional seats via redistricting appear to have fallen short. Several people involved in DeSantis’ 2024 presidential campaign told CNN that his movements in the past 48 hours were interpreted within his orbit as keeping the door open to another White House bid. On Wednesday, DeSantis declined to discuss his future and told CNN he will “be a free man” in January. DeSantis wasn’t the only ambitious Republican rushing to rationalize the midterm losses. Texas Sen. Ted Cruz, who, said Wednesday on his popular “Verdict” podcast after his state saw massive GOP losses that “too many in politics dismissed” affordability concerns — an issue Trump himself regularly insisted was a manufactured problem. “Understandably people were pissed off and elected Republicans didn’t do enough to address their very real pain,” he said. Meanwhile, outgoing Georgia Gov. Brian Kemp, a Trump antagonist, on Wednesday laid out his own vision for the party centered on the “conservative principles of our party.” “It’s time we get back to those principles in the months and years to come,” Kemp wrote. A GOP operative in neighboring South Carolina, another early-nominating state, told CNN after seeing Kemp’s post: “He’s running.” The person noted that Kemp recently appeared in the Palmetto State to help campaign for the Republican gubernatorial candidate there, Attorney General Alan Wilson, who won on Tuesday. To be sure, Vance remains the clear front-runner for the GOP nomination. Primary voters typically are considerably deferential to vice presidents. Vance would bring other advantages to a protracted nomination battle, including a close relationship with the party’s biggest donors after serving as Republican National Committee finance chair for the past 20 months. He also has the backing of Turning Point USA, the organization founded by the late conservative activist Charlie Kirk, that is seen as a turnkey political operation for Vance if he wants it. However, the group’s political influence took a hit in the midterms as well. Republicans suffered heavy losses in states where the group is especially active, and it went all-in on Republican Andy Biggs, who is on track to the lose the Arizona governor race by double digits. A spokesman for Turning Point didn’t return a request for comment. Vance presumably would run with Trump’s support — an endorsement Vance recently said he expects to receive but has yet to come. Trump does not appear especially eager to pass the torch and has at times floated other names as potential successors, most notably Secretary of State Marco Rubio. The former Florida senator remains of favorite of many establishment figures in the GOP and has created new fans among the MAGA faithful, but it’s not clear that he wants to run and has said in the past he wouldn’t go up against Vance. As a key player in Trump’s administration, especially on foreign policy, Rubio could face similar headwinds as Vance running to succeed him. Despite his platform-like statement Wednesday, it isn’t a sure thing that Vance will seek the nomination either. Vance himself has said he would wait until after the midterms to make that decision and close allies have publicly and privately suggested that Tuesday’s outcome is likely to factor into that calculus. Trump said Wednesday he remains in the dark on Vance’s plans. “Maybe he won’t run,” Trump said as he showed off construction for his White House ballroom. “I don’t know who is going to run.” If Vance ultimately forgoes a White House bid, a chaotic race to replace Trump would surely follow. Several members of Trump’s own Cabinet harbor presidential ambitions – including Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy, Jr. and Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth – and it’s unclear they would run unless Vance decided against it. Hegseth is also facing renewed criticism from his party over the war with Iran and could face an impeachment vote in the House as soon as next week, CNN reported Wednesday . The political movements of conservative commentator Tucker Carlson remain a source of intrigue among Republicans as well. Carlson, a close friend of Vance, remains publicly supportive of the vice president and has said he won’t seek the presidency. But he has also floated the creation of a third party, and supporters like former Rep. Marjorie Taylor Greene have encouraged him to run. In Iowa, as voters weighed in on the midterms, some future caucus-goers were already ready to look beyond Trump as they consider who replaces him. “I want to get away from that idea of ‘Trump Republican,’ and just get back to Republican-conservative,” said David McDonald, a 59-year-old meat cutter from Des Moines told CNN. Marion, Iowa, retiree Rich Sidman acknowledged the future of the GOP will come down to how Trump fares over the next two years. “It’s all about the economy, the economy, the economy,” Sidman said. He’s bullish, though, on Vance after seeing him speak during the vice president’s recent campaign swing through Iowa. And if the caucuses were today, that’s who Sidman would vote for. What about DeSantis — who made Iowa a second home in 2023 as he tried to seize the party from Trump? Sidman thought for a moment, then said: “I wouldn’t mind seeing DeSantis either.”

title: Burnham wants to ‘recast’ Chagos Islands deal after US resistance
content: Andy Burnham has said he wants to “recast” the UK’s deal to cede control of the Chagos Islands after resistance from Washington, which said the agreement could instead be modelled on America’s Greenland deal with Denmark . The prime minister told the Economist he wanted “a new discussion” with the US over the disputed islands, which are home to the Diego Garcia military base. The original deal, which was struck by the former prime minister Keir Starmer and would have given sovereignty of the islands to Mauritius, has been in limbo since Donald Trump made clear he opposed it. Burnham said: “We are in discussion with our US friends to see how we might recast the arrangement that better meets their concerns. “We look at the Greenland deal and obviously there was a solution reached there. Now, maybe there is something there we can take from that to see if there’s a solution that works in relation to Diego Garcia. But that is something that we’re very engaged on. We’re working hard on it, but it is challenging.” Starmer’s government signed a treaty to transfer sovereignty to Mauritius while keeping control of the joint UK-US base on Diego Garcia under a 99-year lease. Under the agreement, Mauritius would have received £165m for three years and £120m a year from the fourth year. The agreement was thrown into uncertainty when Trump voiced his opposition to it. Speaking in September after a bilateral meeting with Burnham in New York, the president said : “I don’t support it – I think it’s a terrible deal.” Wes Streeting, the defence secretary, has since said the British government had suspended payments to Mauritius while the UK and US worked on a compromise. He told the BBC: “This deal as it is currently constituted can’t go ahead without American support. So we have to get a deal to a place where it commands American support as well as the agreement of the government of Mauritius and our government.” While Trump was expressing his unhappiness at the Chagos deal, he was striking an agreement with Denmark over Greenland, after months of threats towards the island. Under that agreement, Greenland will remain a Danish territory but the US will be allowed to develop a significant military presence there, while its adversaries will be banned from building their ⁠own bases on the island. Burnham was speaking on his return journey from Antigua, where he attended the Commonwealth heads of government (Chogm) summit. Much of the trip was dominated by demands from Caribbean countries for Britain to pay reparations for slavery, but Burnham insisted his government had helped move the issue on by opening up the possibility of a government apology. “I think we have done something, we’ve achieved something out there,” he said. Burnham will host his own international summit next year when the G20 meets in Manchester. Burnham said the Russian president, Vladimir Putin, would be barred from that meeting, though the Chinese president, Xi Jinping, would be welcome. And obviously he’s coming back 12 years later and he will see a big difference in Manchester. And some of that has been done in partnership with China.” Over the next few weeks, Burnham will prepare for the EU summit in Brussels, which the prime minister says will be a moment for the UK to begin thinking about its longer-term relationship with the bloc and whether it should rejoin. He will also pull together his “10-year plan”, which aides say will lay out his long-term vision for how the UK should change over the next decade, including public control over key parts of the economy. Burnham said the plan, which had been promised for this year, could be delayed until January. He denied recent reports that it would be relatively brief and lacking in detail. “It will be substantial, and it will also be – well, in my view, it will be compelling because I am weaving the different threads together,” he said. “We may go into the new year, to be honest … December or January. I think we will need to leave that open.”

title: Failing Grayling double reports for duty as Reform’s armed forces spokesperson
content: Y ou can make a good case for Nigel Farage having been one of the most consequential British politicians of the 21st century. Without him there would have been no Brexit. And yet it is now beginning to look as if his time has come and gone. The narcissistic qualities that have served him so well now threaten to finish him off. His skin is becoming thinner by the day. All that’s left is reflexive lashing out. A raging against the dying of the light. You’d need to have a heart of stone not to laugh. On Thursday, Nige was at the old Billingsgate fish market in central London for a press conference – not another one – at which he was to unveil his new armed forces spokesperson. Only this would turn out to be a press conference with a difference. Nige would not be taking any questions for the cameras. You couldn’t help but think he was struggling to shake off the humiliation of insisting the pollsters were wrong about the Republicans in the US midterms. Trump would not be smashed, he said. The American voters saw it differently. And now The Donald was proving to be a liability. It’s not just Nige who is suffering. He’s taking his whole team down with him. Not least those former Tory MPs who had thought the Conservatives were dead in the water. Danny Kruger was supposed to be the sensible one. The one who could provide a veneer of intelligence to the Reform project. Yet Nice Danny is rapidly morphing into Desperate Dan: a man now thinking he may have been a bit hasty and made the wrong call. Desperate Dan had been roped in as the warm-up act. Usually the sort of meaningless gig that is delegated to Dicky Tice. It probably wasn’t in the script for Dan to use his five-minute gig to unload his full existential meltdown, but that was what he got. Angry Dan is a sucker for any conspiracy theory. The polls had been rigged to make it look as if Reform was in third place. And John Healey had only resigned as defence secretary so that he could get the job as chancellor in order to dismantle all the armed forces. The madness apogee was reached when Desperate Dan declared that no politician in the whole country knew more about defence than Nige. In a war, Nige would be the first person trying to escape the draft with ingrown toenails. Reform have never even got round to naming a defence spokesperson or showing the slightest interest in the subject. Reform’s attendance in parliament for defence-related matters is pitiful. Nige took centre stage to a standing ovation. There are still a few hardcore believers left. He craves the attention despite the ever-diminishing returns. “The world is more dangerous now than it has been for 80 years,” he said, with his trademark grin. He could be right, though he hadn’t stopped to consider whether Vladimir Putin and Donald Trump – two leaders whom he has openly admired – might have contributed to that. Nige has blamed the Ukraine war on Nato and was all up for joining the US in bombing Iran. The 3.5% of GDP by 2035 was paltry, he continued. Though he didn’t commit to spending any more or saying how the increase would be funded. But help was at hand. Nige had tracked down the one man in the entire armed services who could save the country from its darkest hour. No matter that the RAF had rather overlooked the talents of the wing commander with 40 years’ service. Meet Angus MacIntyre, who last week resigned from the RAF to become Nige’s official wingman. Cue a spectacular double take. Because the man who walked on stage was a dead ringer for Chris Grayling, the former Tory minister who had never yet found a job he couldn’t do worse than anyone else. Failing Grayling made a career out of his own incompetence. Mediocrity was a level of achievement to which he could only aspire. Being Failing Grayling’s double is a cross no man should have to bear but Angus was determined to do his best. He was happy to report for duty as Reform’s shadow minister for the armed forces. This was Angus’s first lie in his new role. Start as you mean to go on. He is not and is never going to be a shadow minister. That role can only ever be done by a Tory as the official opposition. But maybe no one had yet got round to explaining such things to him. Angus was a grunt who operated on a need to know basis. MacIntyre quickly moved on to his CV, which includes spells in the US and at Nato HQ. More lanyard class than man of action. Nor did he quite explain why he had finished his career only as wing commander despite four decades of service. You couldn’t help thinking Angus might have been passed over for promotion several times and that the RAF hadn’t quite appreciated his talents as much as he would have liked. Still, Angus looks as if he has landed in the right place, sounding suitably swivel-eyed about net zero and condemning current attitudes towards the armed forces as “Marxist ideology”. However, it was a little weird that Reform’s new man from the military had nothing to say about either Ukraine or Iran. It would have been good to know if he shared Nige’s admiration for Putin and Trump and whether he, too, looks on not joining the Iran war as a missed opportunity. Nor did he say whether he intended to stand as an MP or who was paying him. Questions, questions. “Have I got the right guy?” Nige asked the audience, as he joined Angus on stage for a last group hug. We will find out soon enough. But my bet would be that Angus may soon be feeling buyer’s remorse. Nige looks as if he is running on empty.
